title: The binding in the morning
hookLine: many read the binding of Isaac each morning, asking for Abraham's devotion

lines: A FATHER, A SON, A KNIFE.
cards: Genesis, chapter twenty-two. God tells Abraham to take his son Isaac up a mountain and offer him there. Abraham rises early, saddles the donkey, splits the wood.
Father and son walk together for three days. On the mountain, Abraham builds an altar, binds his son, and lifts the knife. And an angel calls out and stops him.
People have argued over this story for thousands of years; some of the most honest readers say it frightens them. And many Jews read it every morning, before breakfast.

teach.b: In Hebrew it's the akedah, the binding, from the word for tying Isaac's hands and feet. The old Jewish translation opens the chapter: "God did prove Abraham." A test.
When God calls, Abraham answers, "Here am I," and at the end, when the angel calls, he answers the same way.

teach.h: LAY NOT THY HAND UPON THE LAD.
teach.b: And the angel says: "Lay not thy hand upon the lad." Isaac isn't harmed. Why read it daily?
The custom spread in the later Middle Ages, and the Shulchan Aruch, the sixteenth-century code of Jewish law, calls it good to say each morning.
After it, many prayer books add a request, roughly: just as Abraham held back his compassion to do your will, so may your compassion hold back your anger from us.
Abraham's devotion becomes something his children ask God to remember.
The tradition calls this zechut avot, the merit of the ancestors: what the founders gave still counts for those who come after. Jews read this story many ways.
Some see the height of faith: a person willing to give everything. Others stress the ending: the God of this story stops the knife, and many teachers have read it as a rejection of child sacrifice.
Some live with the question and never settle it. Reading it every morning doesn't settle it either. It keeps the question, and the devotion, close.

how: Many Orthodox prayer books print the akedah (Genesis 22) near the start of the morning service with a request that follows it; some people say it privately each day, while other communities and prayer books leave it out.

that God remember Abraham's devotion and be compassionate to us.

games.why: just as Abraham held back his compassion to do God's will, the request asks God's compassion to hold back anger from his children.

practice: Think of someone, in your family, your history, your neighborhood, who gave something costly for what they believed or loved: a grandparent who crossed an ocean, a parent who worked two jobs, a friend who kept a promise when it hurt.
Picture one moment of that devotion, and ask quietly: what of theirs am I still living on? If you pray, you can ask God to remember them.

wordCard.voice: Akedah. The binding — Genesis twenty-two's story of Isaac bound on the altar, read daily by many Jews, asking God to remember Abraham's devotion.

orig.note: Hebrew: binding, from the verb used for tying Isaac in Genesis 22:9.
